title: Tomato Soup
description: San Marzano tomato soup with bloomed spices and a monter au beurre finish.

changelog.note: Imported from Cody's Claude chat — replaced the placeholder sample.
Precision pass: every step now restates exact amounts at the point of use.
Steps de-quantified: amounts live in the ingredient list only, so instructions stay correct at any serving scale.
Step amounts now render dynamically from the ingredient list via {id} tokens, scaling with the servings selector.

items.note: her signature — it's its own recipe here

steps.text: Melt {butter} in a large pot over medium heat. Add {onion}, diced, and cook until soft and translucent, 8-10 minutes.
steps.why: Sweating — not browning — breaks the onion down sweet and mellow. Browned edges would muddy the tomato's brightness.

steps.text: Add {garlic}, minced, and cook 1 minute until fragrant.
Add {paste} and cook, stirring constantly, 3-4 minutes until it darkens to brick red. It should smell sweet and caramelized, not raw.
steps.why: Raw paste tastes tinny. Toasting caramelizes its sugars and browns it into the deep savory-sweet backbone of the whole pot.

steps.text: Add {basil}, {oregano}, and {paprika} straight into the paste. Stir 30-60 seconds until fragrant.
steps.why: Dried-herb flavors are fat-soluble. Blooming them in hot fat releases what a watery simmer never would.

steps.text: Add {tomatoes} with their juice, breaking them up with a spoon, then {broth}, {sugar}, and a pinch of red pepper flakes if using. Boil, then drop to a simmer for 20-25 minutes.
steps.why: The simmer melds and concentrates everything. Taste before all the sugar goes in — San Marzanos are naturally sweet.

steps.text: Puree completely smooth with an immersion blender, or in batches in a regular blender with the lid vented.
steps.why: Hot liquid in a sealed blender builds steam pressure and erupts. Venting lets it escape.

steps.text: Reduce the heat to low, stir in {cream}, and simmer gently 5 minutes. Do not let it boil again.
steps.why: A boil curdles dairy — the proteins clump past a bare simmer. Low and slow keeps it silky.

steps.text: Off the heat: whisk in {cold-butter}, cold and cubed, one cube at a time until the soup turns glossy (monter au beurre).
steps.why: Cold butter whisked in off-heat emulsifies instead of melting out — suspended fat is what gives the velvet texture and professional sheen. Too much heat and it breaks to grease.

steps.text: Season generously with salt and pepper — it wants more salt than you think.

notes.title: Make ahead
notes.body: The soup holds 3 days refrigerated — but do the cold-butter finish fresh each time you reheat, or the gloss is gone.

plating: Wide bowls. Spiral of basil oil, one crack of black pepper. Croque monsieur alongside when it's that kind of night.
elevations: Drop a parmesan rind in for the simmer, out before blending — quiet umami depth.
A few drops of sherry vinegar at the very end sharpens the whole bowl.
variations: Vegetable broth for a meat-free version.
